cemc-hypatia-2003-01a.prompt: Quentin has a number of square tiles, each measuring $1$ cm by $1$ cm. He tries to put these small square tiles together to form a larger square of side length $n$ cm, but finds that he has $92$ tiles left over. If he had increased the side length of the larger square to $(n + 2)$ cm, he would have been $100$ tiles short of completing the larger square. How many tiles does Quentin have?

cemc-hypatia-2003-01b.prompt: Quentin's friend Rufus arrives with a big pile of identical blocks, each in the shape of a cube. Quentin takes some of the blocks and Rufus takes the rest. Quentin uses his blocks to try to make a large cube with $8$ blocks along each edge, but finds that he is $24$ blocks short. Rufus, on the other hand, manages to exactly make a large cube using all of his blocks. If they use all of their blocks together, they are able to make a complete cube which has a side length that is $2$ blocks longer than Rufus' cube. How many blocks are there in total?

cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.prompt:
Xavier and Yolanda are playing a game starting with some coins arranged in piles. Xavier always goes first, and the two players take turns removing one or more coins from any *one* pile. The player who takes the last coin wins.

If there are two piles of coins with $3$ coins in each pile, show that Yolanda can guarantee that she always wins the game.
cemc-hypatia-2003-02a.answer: Copy strategy: whatever Xavier takes from one pile, Yolanda takes the same number from the other, so the piles are always equal after her move and she takes the last coin.

cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.prompt:
Xavier and Yolanda are playing a game starting with some coins arranged in piles. Xavier always goes first, and the two players take turns removing one or more coins from any *one* pile. The player who takes the last coin wins.

If the game starts with piles of $1$, $2$ and $3$ coins, explain how Yolanda can guarantee that she always wins the game.
cemc-hypatia-2003-02b.answer: After Xavier's first move Yolanda can always leave two equal piles and one empty pile (e.g. $0,2,3 \to 0,2,2$; $1,1,3 \to 1,1,0$; $1,2,2 \to 0,2,2$; $1,2,1 \to 1,0,1$; ...), then she copies Xavier as in (a).

cemc-hypatia-2003-03.prompt: In the diagram, the sphere has a diameter of $10$ cm. Also, the right circular cone has a height of $10$ cm, and its base has a diameter of $10$ cm. The sphere and cone sit on a horizontal surface. If a horizontal plane cuts both the sphere and the cone, the cross-sections will both be circles, as shown. Find the height of the horizontal plane that gives circular cross-sections of the sphere and cone of equal area.

cemc-hypatia-2003-04a.prompt:
Square $ABCD$ has vertices $A(1, 4)$, $B(5, 4)$, $C(5, 8)$, and $D(1, 8)$. From a point $P$ outside the square, a vertex of the square is said to be *visible* if it can be connected to $P$ by a straight line that does not pass through the square. Thus, from any point $P$ outside the square, either two or three of the vertices of the square are visible. The *visible area of P* is the area of the one triangle or the sum of the areas of the two triangles formed by joining $P$ to the two or three visible vertices of the square.

Show that the *visible area* of $P(2, -6)$ is $20$ square units.
cemc-hypatia-2003-04a.answer: Only $A$ and $B$ are visible; $\triangle ABP$ has base $AB = 4$ and height $4 - (-6) = 10$, so area $20$.

cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.prompt:
Square $ABCD$ has vertices $A(1, 4)$, $B(5, 4)$, $C(5, 8)$, and $D(1, 8)$. From a point $P$ outside the square, a vertex of the square is said to be *visible* if it can be connected to $P$ by a straight line that does not pass through the square. Thus, from any point $P$ outside the square, either two or three of the vertices of the square are visible. The *visible area of P* is the area of the one triangle or the sum of the areas of the two triangles formed by joining $P$ to the two or three visible vertices of the square.

Show that the visible area of $Q(11, 0)$ is also $20$ square units.
cemc-hypatia-2003-04b.answer: $A$, $B$, $C$ are visible; $\triangle QBC = \tfrac12(4)(6) = 12$ and $\triangle QBA = \tfrac12(4)(4) = 8$; total $20$.

cemc-hypatia-2003-04c.prompt:
Square $ABCD$ has vertices $A(1, 4)$, $B(5, 4)$, $C(5, 8)$, and $D(1, 8)$. From a point $P$ outside the square, a vertex of the square is said to be *visible* if it can be connected to $P$ by a straight line that does not pass through the square. Thus, from any point $P$ outside the square, either two or three of the vertices of the square are visible. The *visible area of P* is the area of the one triangle or the sum of the areas of the two triangles formed by joining $P$ to the two or three visible vertices of the square.

The set of points $P$ for which the visible area equals $20$ square units is called the *20/20 set*, and is a polygon. Determine the perimeter of the 20/20 set.
